title: Enhancing Final Exam Performance Through Retrieval Practice: Evidence From a Diverse College Sample https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00986283251352475
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), July 29, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Kenneth Barideaux's study testing whether a single brief multiple-choice practice test beats a traditional instructor-led review for boosting final exam performance in a racially and generationally diverse undergraduate sample. The 38-student study found retrieval practice improved overall exam scores across factual, applied, and even unrelated question types, while also reducing students' perceived exam difficulty and self-reported anxiety. Barton frames this within the desirable-difficulties literature: a small dose of effortful recall outperforms passive review, and the benefit generalised across a genuinely diverse sample of students, over a third of whom were first-generation college students. He flags the caveats clearly — this was a quasi-experimental design with a single brief intervention and no measurement of students' independent study habits — but takes from it that even minimal-preparation retrieval practice is worth prioritising ahead of instructor-led review.
points: A single brief multiple-choice practice test outperformed a traditional instructor-led review on final exam scores, across factual, applied, and unrelated questions.
The benefit held across a racially and generationally diverse student sample, supporting retrieval practice as an equitable teaching strategy.
Retrieval practice reduced students' self-reported worry and perceived difficulty around the exam, not just their scores.
The intervention required minimal teacher preparation, making it a low-cost, high-leverage classroom strategy.
Barton cautions that the quasi-experimental design and single, brief, fact-based intervention limit how far the findings generalise to longer courses or richer question types.
quotes: Retrieval practice improved overall exam scores across various question types, including rephrased and applied concepts, and also reduced perceived exam difficulty and anxiety among students.
This learning strategy is simple to implement and requires minimal preparation.
Instructors should encourage retrieval practice both in class and for independent study, especially when students are preparing for formal assessments.
Retrieval practice improves student performance on final exams, benefiting not just factual questions, but also applied and even unrelated questions.
Students who engage in retrieval practice report less worry or anxiety about their exam grade and perceive the exam as less difficult.
This study replicated and extended past findings by showing that a brief retrieval practice activity benefits diverse learners in the classroom.
